summary: The Quraysh leadership imposed a total social and economic boycott on the Banu Hashim and Banu Muttalib clans for their protection of the Prophet ﷺ, forcing them into a mountain pass (Shi'b Abi Talib) for nearly three years of severe hardship and near-starvation.
narrative:
When the Quraysh's attempts to silence or co-opt the Prophet ﷺ through negotiation and persecution of individual Muslims failed, the tribal leadership collectively agreed on a more sweeping measure. They drew up a formal agreement — written on parchment and hung inside the Kaabah — imposing a total boycott on the Banu Hashim and Banu Abd al-Muttalib clans. The agreement prohibited any commercial transactions, intermarriage, or social contact with the clan members unless they handed over Muhammad ﷺ for execution.

Ibn Hisham records the full scope of the boycott in detail, drawing from Ibn Ishaq. The document was drafted and signed by the leading men of the Quraysh. The Banu Hashim and their allies were forced to withdraw to the Shi'b (mountain pass or ravine) of Abu Talib — a valley outside the boundaries of Makkah proper — where they lived in a state of siege. The boycott lasted approximately three years, from approximately 616 to 619 CE.

The conditions during the boycott were severe. Al-Tabari records, through multiple chains, that the beleaguered clan was reduced to eating leaves from trees and leather. Ibn Hisham mentions the cries of hungry children could be heard from within the pass. Food was sometimes smuggled in secretly by sympathizers; Hakim ibn Hizam, the nephew of Khadijah (RA), is specifically mentioned as one who secretly sent grain to his aunt. Abu Jahl tried to intercept even these acts of mercy.

Khadijah (RA) spent much of her considerable wealth supporting the Muslims through this period. Ibn Sa'd notes that by the time the boycott ended, her fortune had been largely exhausted — a sacrifice she made willingly. The hardship of the boycott is considered by scholars to have contributed to her declining health, which led to her death shortly after the boycott ended.

The boycott was eventually broken not through Muslim resistance but through the consciences of several Quraysh men who were uncomfortable with its extremity. Ibn Hisham records that five men — among them Hisham ibn Amr, Zuhayr ibn Abi Umayyah, al-Mut'im ibn Adi, Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham, and Zama'ah ibn al-Aswad — agreed to annul the document. When they went to the Kaabah to announce this publicly, Abu Talib told them that the Prophet ﷺ had been informed that the parchment itself had been eaten by termites, leaving only the phrase 'In Your name, O Allah' at the top intact. When the parchment was retrieved and inspected, this was found to be true — a remarkable detail recorded by Ibn Hisham and considered by later scholars as a sign of divine intervention, though al-Tabari notes different accounts of the sequence of events.

The end of the boycott in approximately 619 CE brought relief, but the community had been severely weakened. Two of the Prophet's greatest supporters — Khadijah (RA) and Abu Talib — would die in the same year, earning it the title 'the Year of Sorrow.'
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah, Vol. 1 — The Shi'b and the Boycott Document
